# The Vanishing Night

There is a version of the night that most people alive today will never meet. It begins when the last light dies—not dimmed, not replaced by the pale wash of a screen, but extinguished—and it arrives slowly. At first there is only a blackness that is not quite black: the ground beneath your feet becomes a suggestion, the horizon a guess. Then, if you are patient and far enough from any city, your eyes begin their ancient chemistry. Over the next half hour, a pigment called rhodopsin regenerates in your retinal cells, and your sensitivity to faint light improves by many thousands of times. The sky opens. Not a handful of bright stars struggling through haze, but thousands upon thousands, arranged in depth, the Milky Way arching overhead like smoke frozen mid-pour, dense enough in places to cast a faint shadow on the ground. This was the night our ancestors knew. For them it was not scenery. It was the governing fact of half of all existence.

Most of us have traded that night away, and mostly without noticing. According to the most comprehensive atlas of night-sky brightness ever assembled, the Milky Way is hidden from more than a third of humanity—including sixty percent of Europeans and nearly eighty percent of North Americans. More than four in five people worldwide live under light-polluted skies. What replaces the stars is skyglow: artificial light scattered through the atmosphere into a luminous dome over every population center, bright enough to erase all but the brightest points of light. Recent measurements suggest the problem is accelerating rather than improving—that the glow above our heads may be brightening by something close to ten percent each year. And in 1994, when an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, residents of the suddenly dark city reportedly called police stations and observatories to ask about a strange, enormous, silvery cloud that had appeared overhead. It was the Milky Way. Some of them were meeting it for the first time in their lives.

It is worth remembering how recently this happened, and how completely the older night structured human life. For most of history, darkness fell like a wall. Work stopped. Cities locked their gates; the very word *curfew* descends from *cuevrefeu*, the signal to cover fires. Watchmen patrolled with lanterns and bells, and households banked their hearths and settled into a darkness we can barely imagine, broken only by rushlight and tallow candle—flames feeble enough that reading after sundown was a luxury of the rich. The night had its own laws, its own economy, its own dangers and freedoms. It was the time of ghosts and fairies, of lovers and thieves, of worship and storytelling. Whole professions existed to manage it: linkboys who carried torches to guide travelers, bellmen who cried the hours, lamplighters who made their rounds at dusk. To live then was to know two worlds, and the boundary between them was absolute. You crossed it every evening whether you wished to or not, and what waited on the other side was genuinely other—unlit, unmapped, humming with presences both imagined and real.

One of the strangest discoveries about that vanished world concerns sleep itself. The historian Roger Ekirch, sifting through diaries, court records, medical texts, and devotional manuals going back centuries, found that pre-industrial Westerners did not sleep the way we do. They slept in two segments. After a few hours of "first sleep," people woke naturally into a quiet interval that lasted an hour or more—a state they regarded as ordinary and even valuable. Documents refer to it plainly: the "watch," the time between "first sleep" and "morning sleep." People prayed; many prayer books included specific offices for those midnight hours. They talked, smoked, read by embers, visited neighbors, tended the fire, made love—Ekirch found physicians advising that conception was most likely during this drowsy interlude. Then they sank back into "second sleep" until dawn. This bimodal rhythm appears not just in European sources but in accounts from other cultures, and modern sleep researchers have found hints of it in controlled experiments: deprive people of artificial evening light and their sleep begins, within weeks, to split down the middle again. Our consolidated eight hours, it turns out, may be an artifact of the light bulb—a habit less than two centuries old, mistaken for human nature.

None of this is an argument against artificial light, which deserves its reputation as one of civilization's genuine miracles. Electric lighting extended the day for reading and study; it made streets safer and hospitals operable around the clock; it freed millions from dependence on daylight for their livelihoods. When gaslight came to London in the early nineteenth century, crowds reportedly gathered to marvel at the glowing pipes. When whole districts first switched on electric arcs, newspapers described the astonishment of streets bright as noon at midnight. The ability to abolish darkness at will is among the great liberations of the modern age, and no honest account wishes it undone. The question is not whether we should have light, but whether we ever paused to ask what we were trading for it—because the trade was made wholesale, street by street, decade by decade, without anyone tallying the cost on the other side of the ledger.

The cost has a name now: light pollution, though the term undersells it, since nothing is polluted so much as our sense of proportion. Only a fraction of the light we emit ever reaches the ground usefully. Much of it spills sideways and upward, unshielded, glaring, aimed at nothing. It scatters off air molecules and aerosols and returns to earth as that diffuse orange-white dome, bright enough within cities to hide every star but the planets and a few stubborn bright ones. Astronomers noticed first—they measure the damage professionally—but the deeper losses registered elsewhere, in places no one thought to look: along coastlines, in treetops, inside our own skulls.

Consider what happens each summer on beaches where sea turtles still nest. Hatchlings emerge from the sand at night and instinctively scramble toward the brighter horizon—which, for millions of years, meant the moonlit sea. Today a beachfront strip of hotels and streetlights can outshine the ocean, and thousands of baby turtles turn the wrong way, crawling inland toward roads and pools and death, or circling in exhaustion until dawn predators find them. Consider the moths spiraling into porch lights. We barely understand why they do it; one recent theory holds that flying insects instinctively keep their backs toward the brightest point in the sky, using it to stay level, and that our lamps trap them in endless corrective loops. Whatever the mechanism, insects near lights pay dearly, and insects anchor food webs everywhere. Consider migratory birds, navigating at night by stars and magnetic fields, drawn off course by city glare and killed by the hundreds of millions annually in collisions with illuminated buildings. When Chicago dims its lakeshore towers during migration, researchers have measured collisions falling by an order of magnitude. Even trees respond: saplings under streetlights hold their leaves later into autumn, their seasonal clocks scrambled by a day that never ends.

And consider ourselves. Human bodies evolved under a strict alternation of bright days and dark nights, and the machinery that keeps time inside us still expects it. Darkness triggers the pineal gland to release melatonin, the hormone that ushers in biological night; light—especially the blue-rich wavelengths our screens and modern LEDs emit most efficiently—suppresses it. Chronic exposure to light at the wrong hours is implicated in disrupted sleep, metabolic problems, and mood disorders, and worse: the World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies shift work that disrupts circadian rhythms as a probable human carcinogen. We are, in effect, running an ancient operating system under conditions it was never built for, and then medicating the symptoms—sleeping pills, caffeine, antidepressants—while leaving the underlying condition untouched. The remedy, where it is available, is almost embarrassingly simple: real darkness, on schedule, every night.

But the deepest losses are harder to measure than hormones or hatchlings. For most of human history, the night sky was the shared text of our species. Calendars hung there; planting and harvest, festivals and fasts followed the moon. Every culture projected its stories onto the stars, and navigators read them like scripture. Polynesian voyagers crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific using star paths memorized as sequences of rising and setting points—knowledge so complete that in 1976 the canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti and back using traditional wayfinding alone, reviving a science that had survived only in fragments. Farmers steered by the Dipper's handle marking the seasons. Enslaved people fleeing north through unfamiliar country looked for the North Star. The sky was infrastructure, almanac, cathedral, and compass at once. Losing it is not like losing a pretty view. It is more like a society forgetting how to read.

Artists understood what was at stake before scientists did. The nocturne—John Field invented the musical form, Chopin perfected it—was an attempt to translate darkness into sound: hushed, wandering, intimate. Whistler painted the Thames at night in veils of blue-green mist and called those paintings nocturnes too, insisting they were arrangements of color rather than pictures of things; when the critic Ruskin accused him of flinging a pot of paint in the public's face, Whistler sued and won a farthing. And in June 1889, in the asylum at Saint-Rémy, Vincent van Gogh painted the view from his iron-barred window—or rather, painted what the night meant, since he worked from memory and imagination as much as observation, setting eleven stars swirling over sleeping Provence with a cypress stitching earth to sky. He had written to his brother that looking at stars always made him dream, as simply and naively as the black dots on a map of France. He knew the night sky was a language. He was trying to speak it back.

There is a quieter argument for darkness, one that has less to do with data than with the shape of a life. Vision itself requires it: the eye that stares at brightness sees nothing else; only in the dark do faint things appear. Every photographer knows this, and every mystic. Darkness is where the mind stops performing and starts conversing with itself—hence the peculiar honesty of insomnia, the strange lucidity of lying awake at three in the morning, the reason so much of what we truly think arrives unscheduled, on the edge of sleep. A life without darkness is not only physiologically deranged; it is psychologically impoverished. It leaves no room for the unwitnessed self, the self that exists when no one, including oneself, is watching. We have engineered away the night's emptiness and filled it with content, and we wonder why we feel watched even when alone. The dark was the one place the world stopped making demands. We sold it cheaply, and we did not notice the sale.

Yet the news is not all bad, because darkness turns out to be one of the few environmental wounds that heals quickly when the cause is removed. Switch off a light and the stars return that same night—no decades-long recovery, no contaminated soil to remediate. This reversibility has inspired a quiet counter-movement. The International Dark-Sky Association, founded in 1988 by two astronomers, now certifies dark sky places around the world: parks, reserves, entire communities that have rewritten their lighting codes. Flagstaff, Arizona, became the first International Dark Sky City in 2001, having shielded its streetlights since the 1950s to protect the observatories on its mountaintops. The fixes are mundane and cheap: full cutoff fixtures that aim light downward, warmer bulbs, timers and motion sensors, lights that exist only where and when they serve someone. None of this means returning to the tallow-candle world. It means treating light like what it is—a powerful tool that, like any tool, becomes waste and harm the moment it misses its target.

New threats keep arriving, though. The switch to energy-efficient LEDs, meant to shrink our footprint, initially made skyglow worse, because blue-rich white light scatters more readily and because cheaper light invited more of it. And the night above the atmosphere is filling up: tens of thousands of satellites launched and planned in vast constellations, glinting trails that streak astronomical images and add a moving shimmer to even pristine skies. Astronomers have negotiated darker coatings and lower orbits, but the trend line is unmistakable. We are close to losing, everywhere and forever, the sight that prompted every cosmology our species ever devised—the sight that made us ask, in every language we have ever spoken, what those lights are and what we are to them. There ought to be a word for that kind of loss. There may not be, because we have never had to name it before.

What can one person do? More than it might seem. Shield the lights you control; choose warm bulbs; put lights on sensors and timers so they shine only when needed; support dark-sky ordinances in your town; visit the remaining dark places, because visibility is protection. And then, at least once, go and see what all the fuss protects. Drive past the last suburbs on a moonless night, park somewhere safe and open, and give yourself the half hour your eyes require. Do not photograph it; cameras cannot hold it anyway. Just stand there while the sky performs its slow reveal, until the band of the galaxy emerges and the stars thicken past counting, and you feel the peculiar vertigo that struck the Angelenos in 1994—the vertigo of discovering that an enormous, ancient thing has been overhead the whole time, patiently waiting behind a curtain we installed ourselves.

Our ancestors crossed into that darkness every evening of their lives, carrying their small flames into a world twice the size of the daylit one. We have abolished the crossing, and gained much, and forgotten what waits on the other side. But the night is patient; it asks nothing of us except that we stop shining for a little while. Somewhere tonight—above a reserve in New Zealand, a desert in Chile, a stretch of open ocean—the Milky Way is casting faint shadows on the ground, exactly as it did for every generation before electricity, exactly as it will for every generation after, if we decide, while it is still a decision rather than a memory, that this inheritance is worth keeping. Keeping it requires almost nothing: a shielded lamp here, a dimmed screen there, a town willing to aim its light at the ground instead of the sky. And it gives back the oldest spectacle our species has ever known. All we have to do is look up—and mean it. Let there be dark.
